question: What are the walls of the middle ear?
search_query: What are the walls of the middle ear?
answer:
The lateral wall contains the tympanic membrane, chorda tympani nerve, and malleus [Lecture 16b - Middle Ear > III. Middle Ear (Tympanic Cavity) > 3. Walls of the Middle Ear].
The posterior wall includes the aditus to the mastoid antrum, posterior canaliculus for the chorda tympani nerve, and stapedius muscle [Lecture 16b - Middle Ear > III. Middle Ear (Tympanic Cavity) > 3. Walls of the Middle Ear].
The inferior wall has the tympanic canaliculus for the tympanic nerve of CN IX and vascular structures (internal carotid artery and jugular vein) (flagged for review, see fact-check) [Lecture 16b - Middle Ear > III. Middle Ear (Tympanic Cavity) > 3. Walls of the Middle Ear].
The medial wall contains the oval window, closed by the stapes footplate, and the round window, closed by membrane [Lecture 16b - Middle Ear > III. Middle Ear (Tympanic Cavity) > 3. Walls of the Middle Ear].
The anterior wall contains openings for the auditory tube and the tensor tympani muscle [Lecture 16b - Middle Ear > III. Middle Ear (Tympanic Cavity) > 3. Walls of the Middle Ear].

question: What does the sartorius do?
search_query: What does the sartorius do?
answer:
The sartorius, or "taylor" muscle, flexes the knee [Lecture 08 - Anterior and Medial Thigh > Muscles of the Anterior Compartment > Sartorius]. It also flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the hip [Lecture 08 - Anterior and Medial Thigh > Muscles of the Anterior Compartment > Sartorius]. This combination of actions allows for sitting cross-legged [OpenStax A&P 2e §11.6]. It serves as a cover for the adductor canal [Lecture 08 - Anterior and Medial Thigh > Anterior and Medial Thigh > Adductor (Subsartorial) Canal].

question: Which muscles make up the rotator cuff?
search_query: Which muscles make up the rotator cuff?
answer:
The rotator cuff consists of four intrinsic muscles: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis [Lecture 04 - The Shoulder > Scapular Region > The Rotator Cuff], [OpenStax A&P 2e §11.5]. These muscles move the humerus relative to the scapula [Lecture 04 - The Shoulder > Scapular Region > The Rotator Cuff]. They hold the humeral head in the glenoid cavity and act as dynamic ligaments [OpenStax A&P 2e §9.6]. Supraspinatus is the most common muscle affected in rotator cuff tears [Lecture 04 - The Shoulder > The Rotator Cuff > Supraspinatus].

answer:

question: What are the steps to expose the femoral triangle?
search_query: What are the steps to expose the femoral triangle?
answer:
1. Clean and identify the sartorius muscle [Dissection Guide, Class 15, slide 6].
2. Remove some fascia lata to clearly identify the femoral triangle and its boundaries: the inguinal ligament, sartorius muscle, and adductor longus muscle [Dissection Guide, Class 15, slide 6].
3. Bluntly dissect the femoral triangle to expose the lymph nodes, femoral vein, femoral artery, and femoral nerve (from medial to lateral) [Dissection Guide, Class 15, slide 7].
4. Identify the femoral sheath, noting that the branched femoral nerve is not part of it [Dissection Guide, Class 15, slide 7].
5. Clean the femoral artery and vein, then identify the lateral and medial circumflex femoral arteries and the deep femoral artery [Dissection Guide, Class 15, slides 8-9].
6. Remove smaller, deeper veins if they obscure the view [Dissection Guide, Class 15, slides 8-9].
7. Identify the pectineus and iliopsoas muscles in the floor of the femoral triangle [Dissection Guide, Class 15, slides 8-9].

question: How do I remove the gluteus maximus?
search_query: How do I remove the gluteus maximus?
answer:
1. Separate the gluteus maximus and medius by pushing fingers into the space between them [Dissection Guide, Class 14, slide 6].
2. Cut the gluteus maximus close to the posterior surfaces of the sacrum, coccyx, and ilium [Dissection Guide, Class 14, slide 6].
3. Detach the muscle from the sacrotuberous ligament [Dissection Guide, Class 14, slide 6].
4. Reflect the muscle laterally toward the greater trochanter [Dissection Guide, Class 14, slide 6].
5. Cut gluteal nerves and vessels close to their attachments on the underside of the muscle [Dissection Guide, Class 14, slide 6].

question: How do I identify the piriformis and the sciatic nerve?

answer:
1. Identify the piriformis muscle as it passes through the greater sciatic foramen [Dissection Guide, Class 14, slides 7-8].
2. Identify the sciatic nerve inferior to the piriformis [Dissection Guide, Class 14, slides 7-8].

question: How do I open the carpal tunnel?
search_query: How do I open the carpal tunnel?
answer:
1. Identify the flexor retinaculum between the thenar and hypothenar eminences [Dissection Guide, Class 10, slide 11].
2. Insert a probe from proximal to distal deep to the flexor retinaculum into the carpal tunnel [Dissection Guide, Class 10, slide 11].
3. Carefully cut the retinaculum, using the probe to protect the structures inside the carpal tunnel from being severed [Dissection Guide, Class 10, slide 11].
Observe that the median nerve and tendons of flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum superficialis, and flexor digitorum profundus go through the tunnel [Dissection Guide, Class 10, slide 11].

question: How do I remove the brain?
search_query: How do I remove the brain?
answer:
1. Position the cadaver supine with the head hanging over the table edge [Dissection Guide, Class 31, slide 2].
2. Make mid-sagittal and coronal incisions and reflect the flaps [Dissection Guide, Class 31, slide 2].
3. Detach and reflect temporalis muscles, scrape the skull clean, and mark a circle using a rubber band [Dissection Guide, Class 31, slide 3].
4. Saw along the lines into the foramen magnum, preserving vertebral arteries, and remove the bone [Dissection Guide, Class 31, slide 7].
5. Cut the dura along saw lines and reflect it to expose the hemispheres [Dissection Guide, Class 31, slide 9].
6. Cut the falx cerebri attachment at the crista galli and pull it superiorly and posteriorly [Dissection Guide, Class 31, slide 10].
7. Cut the tentorium cerebelli near the petrous temporal bone, lifting the posterior brain to do so [Dissection Guide, Class 31, slides 11-12].

question: What is Broca's area?
search_query: What is Broca's area?
answer:
Broca's area is a functional neuroanatomical region located in the inferior frontal gyrus [Web: MeSH: Broca Area (NLM MeSH)]. It comprises the pars triangularis and the pars opercularis [Web: MeSH: Broca Area (NLM MeSH)]. This region is essential for the production of language and speech [Web: MeSH: Broca Area (NLM MeSH)]. Damage to this area is linked to apraxia and Broca aphasia [Web: MeSH: Broca Area (NLM MeSH)].

question: What is the glomus tympanicum?
search_query: What is the glomus tympanicum?
answer:
The glomus tympanicum is an ovoid, highly vascular body containing chemoreceptive tissue located near the tympanic cavity [Web: MeSH: Glomus Tympanicum (NLM MeSH)]. It originates from neural crest tissue and belongs to the diffuse neuroendocrine system [Web: MeSH: Glomus Tympanicum (NLM MeSH)]. This tissue can be the site of a rare neoplasm known as a glomus tympanicum tumor [Web: MeSH: Glomus Tympanicum Tumor (NLM MeSH)].
